Jordan Lee's own access role on that calendar is "writer" (not owner, not reader).
The calendar's ACL includes an entry for "the design team" as a shared party (a team/group, not an individual).

turn2.differences: The author's three conditions are a faithful, if more coarsely grouped, restatement of my six step-1 conditions: c1 = name match; c2 folds together \"appears on Jordan's calendar list\" and \"Jordan's own role is writer\"; c3 folds together \"has a design-team ACL entry\" and \"that entry's role is writer\". No condition is added, dropped, or reinterpreted — the grouping just merges pairs that always travel together in this request. The only thing the author's list omits is the action itself (set hidden=true), but that's the verb of the request, not a filter on which record it refers to, so it isn't something a \"condition\" list would need to state.

ambiguity_effects.explain: In principle "the design team" could denote any group with "design" in its name or display label, but the record set contains exactly one such group (design-team@northwind.example) and no rival naming variant, so there is nothing for a careful reader to actually hesitate over here.

ambiguity_effects.phrase: shared with the design team as a writer
ambiguity_effects.explain: Grammatically "as a writer" attaches to the design team (the nearer, and only, noun in that clause) describing the role granted to them, not a redundant restatement of Jordan's own role from the earlier clause — so a careful reader settles on one reading. But if someone did (wrongly) read it as merely reiterating Jordan's role and dropped the requirement that the design team's role be writer, team-launch@northwind.example would satisfy the resulting weaker condition (it is shared with design-team, just as reader), so the misreading would add a second, incorrect match.

turn2.naturalness_note: The phrasing is a bit dense (\"the Team Calendar that I have writer access to ... and that's shared with the design team as a writer\"), but that density is exactly the kind a real user produces when they know several calendars share the generic name \"Team Calendar\" and want to pin down the right one by access role and sharing — it doesn't read like an artificial test construction.
